key_insight: The paper proposes learning game-playing agents from synthetic experience, reducing dependence on massive human demonstrations. It aims to make training more scalable and better able to cover the diverse, dynamic states seen in games.
problem_solved: Game agents need broad experience to handle visually rich, highly dynamic environments, but collecting large-scale demonstrations is expensive and often misses many important game states. The paper addresses the lack of scalable training environments and limited coverage in current game-agent pipelines.
method: Generate synthetic experience to supplement or replace sparse real demonstrations.
Train computer-use/game agents on diverse simulated gameplay states and interactions.
Use this synthetic data to improve robustness across complex visuals, mechanics, and edge-case scenarios.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a more scalable path to training agents for complex digital environments without requiring exhaustive human gameplay data. It could improve generalization, reduce data collection costs, and accelerate development of adaptable game and computer-use agents.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing synthetic experience generation -> agent training -> game evaluation.
A before/after comparison of human-demo-only training versus synthetic-experience training.
An environment/state coverage heatmap illustrating broader state diversity.
Icons representing keyboard, mouse, screen, and game worlds to show computer-use control.
paper_title: Player-1: Learning to Play from Synthetic Experience
paper_authors: Mingyu Ouyang, Yiran Wang, Siyuan Hu, Xingyilang Yin, Huiqiang Sun
